Coherence of Type Class Resolution Price: DOI: 10.1145/3341695 Journal: PACMPL Volume: 3 ICFP 91 8 CCS: Theory of computation Type theory CCS: Software and its engineering Correctness CCS: Software and its engineering Functional languages
Gert-Jan Bottu, Ningning Xie, Koar Marntirosian, Tom Schrijvers

Abstract
. Elaboration-based type class resolution, as found in languages like Haskell, Mercury and PureScript, is generally nondeterministic: there can be multiple ways to satisfy a wanted constraint in terms of global instances and locally given constraints. Coherence is the key property that keeps this sane; it guarantees that, despite the nondeterminism, programs still behave predictably. Even though elaboration-based resolution is generally assumed coherent, as far as we know, there is no formal proof of this property in the presence of sources of nondeterminism, like superclasses and flexible contexts. This paper provides a formal proof to remedy the situation. The proof is non-trivial because the semantics elaborates resolution into a target language where different elaborations can be distinguished by contexts that do not have a source language counterpart. Inspired by the notion of full abstraction, we present a two-step strategy that first elaborates nondeterministically into an intermediate language that preserves contextual equivalence, and then deterministically elaborates from there into the target language. We use an approach based on logical relations to establish contextual equivalence and thus coherence for the first step of elaboration, while the second step’s determinism straightforwardly preserves this coherence property.



As a guide to the reader, we present the source language

{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{\textbf{{TC}}}}
in
blue
, the intermediate language
{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{{D}}}}

in
green
and the target language
{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{\lx@text@lbrace\lx@text@rbrace}}}
in
red
.
We thus encourage the reader to view / print this paper in color.

1.
Introduction

Type classes were initially introduced in Haskell
(
Peyton Jones 2003
)

by Wadler and Blott
(
Wadler and Blott 1989
)
to
make ad-hoc overloading less ad hoc, and they have since become one of Haskell’s
core abstraction features.
Moreover, their resounding success has spread far beyond Haskell: several
languages have adopted them (e.g., Mercury
(
Henderson et al. 1996
)
,
Coq
(
Sozeau and Oury 2008
)
, PureScript
(
Freeman 2017
)
, Lean
(
de Moura et al. 2015
)
),
and they have inspired various alternative language features (e.g., Scala’s
implicits
(
Martin Odersky and
Venners 2008
;
Odersky et al. 2017
)
, Rust’s traits
(
Mozilla Research 2017
)
, C++’s
concepts
(
Gregor et al. 2006
)
, Agda’s instance
arguments
(
Devriese and
Piessens 2011
)
).

Type classes have also received a lot of attention from researchers with many
proposals for extensions and improvements, including
functional dependencies
(
Jones 2000
)
, associated
types
(
Chakravarty et al. 2005
)
, quantified
constraints
(
Bottu et al. 2017
)
among other extensions.

Given the extensive attention that type classes have received, it may be
surprising that the metatheory of their elaboration-based semantics
(
Hall
et al. 1996
)
has not yet been exhaustively
studied. In particular, as far as we know, while there have been many
informal arguments, the formal notion of
coherence
has never been proven.

Reynolds 1991
has defined coherence as follows:

“When a programming language has a sufficiently rich type structure, there can
be more than one proof of the same typing judgment; potentially this can lead
to semantic ambiguity since the semantics of a typed language is a function of
such proofs. When no such ambiguity arises, we say that the language is
coherent.”

Type classes give rise to two main (potential) sources of incoherence. The first
source are
ambiguous type schemes
, such as that of the function
foo
:

> foo :: (Show a, Read a) => String -> String
> foo s = show (read s)

The type scheme of
foo
requires that the type with which
a

will be instantiated must have
Show
and
Read
instances. This
restriction alone is too permissive, because the type part
(
String -> String
) of
foo
’s type scheme is not
sufficient for a deterministic instantiation of
a
from the calling
context.

a
can thus be instantiated arbitrarily to any
type with
Show
and
Read
instances. Yet, the choice of type
may lead to a different behavior of
show
and
read
, and thus
of
foo
as a whole. For instance,
foo "1"
yields
"1"

when
a
is instantiated to
Int
, and
"1.0"
when it is
instantiated to
Float
. To rule out this source of incoherence,

Jones 1993
requires type schemes to be unambiguous and has formally proven
that, for his system, this guarantees coherence.

The second source of ambiguity arises from the type class resolution mechanism
itself. Such mechanisms check
whether a particular type class constraint holds.
Usually, they are styled after resolution-based proof
search in logic, where type class instances act as Horn clauses and type scheme
constraints as additional facts.
Generally, this process is nondeterministic, but languages like Haskell, Mercury
or PureScript contain it by
requiring that type class instances do not overlap with
each other or with locally given constraints.
Nevertheless, superclasses remain as a source of nondeterminism; indeed, a superclass
constraint can be resolved through any of its subclass constraints. Hence,
in the presence of superclasses, type class resolution should properly be
considered as a potential source for incoherence. Moreover, overlap between
locally wanted constraints and global instances is often allowed (e.g., through
GHC’s
FlexibleContexts
pragma), but a formal argument
for its harmlessness is also lacking.
Jones 1993
considered neither of these
aspects and simply assumed the coherence of resolution as a given.

Morris 2014
side-steps these issues with a denotational
semantics that is disconnected from the original elaboration-based semantics
and its implementations (e.g., Hugs and GHC).

This paper aims to fill this gap in the metatheory of programming languages
featuring type classes, including industrial grade languages such as Haskell, by formally
establishing that elaboration-based type class resolution is coherent in the presence of
superclasses and flexible contexts. The proof of this property is considerably complicated by the
indirect, elaboration-based approach that is used to give meaning to programs
with type classes.
Indeed, the meaning of such programs is commonly given in terms of their
translation to a core language
(
Hall
et al. 1996
)
, like System F, the
meaning of which is defined in
the form of an operational semantics.
In this translation process, type classes are elaborated into explicitly passed
function dictionaries.
These dictionaries can, however, often be constructed in more than one way,
resulting in multiple possible translations for a single program.
The problem is that different
translations of the same source program actually may have different meanings
in the core language. The reason for this discrepancy is that the core language is more expressive
than the source language and admits programs — that cannot be expressed in
the source language — in which the different dictionaries can be distinguished.

We solve this problem with a new two-step approach that splits the
problem into two subproblems. The midway point is an intermediate language that
makes type class dictionaries explicit, but—inspired by fully abstract
compilation—cannot distinguish between different elaborations from the same
source language term
(
Abadi 1999
)
. We use a logical-relations approach to show that the
nondeterministic elaboration from the source language to this intermediate
language is coherent. Showing coherence for the elaboration from the
intermediate language to the target language is much simpler, because we can
formulate it in a deterministic fashion.

In summary, the contributions of this work are:

•

We present a simple calculus
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{\textbf{{TC}}}}
with full-blown type class resolution (incl.
superclasses), which isolates nondeterministic resolution. Furthermore, we
present an elaboration from
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{\textbf{{TC}}}}
to the target language
{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{\lx@text@lbrace\lx@text@rbrace}}}
, System F with
records, which are used to encode dictionaries.

•

We present an intermediate language
{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{{D}}}}
with explicit dictionary-passing.
This language enforces the uniqueness of dictionaries, which captures
the intention of type class instances. We study its metatheory,
and define a logical relation to prove contextual equivalence.

•

We present elaborations from
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{\textbf{{TC}}}}
to
{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{{D}}}}
and from
{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{{D}}}}
to

{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{\lx@text@lbrace\lx@text@rbrace}}}
, and prove that a direct translation from
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{\textbf{{TC}}}}
to
{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{\lx@text@lbrace\lx@text@rbrace}}}
can
always be decomposed into an equivalent translation through
{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{{D}}}}
.

•

We prove coherence of the elaboration between
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{\textbf{{TC}}}}
and
{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{{D}}}}
, using
logical relations.

•

We prove that coherence is also preserved through the elaboration from

{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{{D}}}}
to
{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{\lx@text@lbrace\lx@text@rbrace}}}
. As a consequence, by combining this with the previous
result, we prove that the elaboration between
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{\textbf{{TC}}}}
and
{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{\lx@text@lbrace\lx@text@rbrace}}}
is
coherent.
The latter coherence result implies coherence of elaboration-based
type class resolution in the presence of superclasses and flexible contexts.

The full formalization and coherence proof can be found in the accompanying 122-page appendix.

The purpose of our work is twofold:

1)

To develop a proof technique to establish coherence of type class
resolution.
Because this result is achieved on a minimal calculus, this work becomes a
basis for researchers investigating type class extensions and larger
languages, as well as their impact on coherence.

2)

To present a formal proof of coherence for language designers considering
to adopt type classes.
In doing so, we show that the informally trivial argument for the coherence of
type class resolution is surprisingly hard to formalize.

2.
Overview

This section provides some background on dictionary-passing elaboration of type
class resolution and discusses the potential nondeterminism introduced by
superclasses and local constraints. We then briefly introduce our calculi and
discuss the key ideas of the coherence proof. Throughout the section we use
Haskell-like syntax as the source language for examples, and to simplify our
informal discussion we use the same syntax without type classes as the target
language.

2.1.
Dictionary-Passing Elaboration

A program is coherent if it has exactly one meaning — i.e., its semantics is
unambiguously determined. For type classes this is not as straightforward as it
seems, because their dynamic semantics are not expressed directly but rather by
type-directed elaboration into a simpler language without type classes
such as System F. Thus the dynamic semantics of type classes are given
indirectly as the dynamic semantics of their elaborated forms.

> class Eq a where
> (==) :: a -> a -> Bool
>
> instance Eq Int where
> (==) = primEqInt
>
> instance (Eq a, Eq b) => Eq (a, b) where
> (x1,y1) == (x2,y2) = x1 == x2 && y1 == y2
>
> refl :: Eq a => a -> Bool
> refl x = x == x
>
> main :: Bool
> main = refl (5,42)

Example 1 (
Program with type classes.
).

Basic Elaboration.

Consider the small program with type classes in Example
1
. We declare
a type class
Eq
and instances for the
Int
and pair types. The
function
refl
trivially tests whether an expression is equivalent to
itself, which is called in
main
.

The dictionary-passing elaboration translates this program into a System F-like
core language that does not feature type classes. The main idea of the
elaboration is to map a type class declaration onto a datatype that contains the
method implementations, a so-called
(function) dictionary
.

> data EqD a = EqD { (==) :: a -> a -> Bool }

Then simple instances give rise to dictionary values:

> eqInt :: EqD Int
> eqInt = EqD { (==) = primEqInt }

Instances with a non-empty context are translated to functions that take context dictionaries
to the instance dictionary.

> eqPair :: (EqD a, EqD b) -> Eq (a,b)
> eqPair (da, db) =
> EqD { (==) = \(x1,y1) (x2,y2) -> (==) da x1 x2 && (==) db y1 y2 }

Functions with qualified types, like
refl
, are translated to
functions that take explicit dictionaries as arguments.

> refl :: EqD a -> a -> Bool
> refl d x = (==) d x x

Finally, calls to functions with a qualified type are mapped to calls that
explicitly pass the appropriate dictionary.

> main :: Bool
> main = refl (eqPair eqInt eqInt) (5,42)

Elaboration of Superclasses.

Superclasses require a small extension to the above elaboration scheme.
Consider the small program in Example
2
where
Sub1
is a
subclass of
Base
. The function
test1
has
Sub1 a
in the
context and calls
sub1
and
base
in its definition.

The standard approach to encode superclass is to embed the superclass dictionary
in that of the subclass. For this case,
Sub1D a
contains a field

super1
that points to the superclass:

> data BaseD a = BaseD { base :: a -> Bool }
> data Sub1D a = Sub1D { super1 :: BaseD a
> , sub1 :: a -> Bool }

This way we can extract the superclass from the subclass when needed. The
function
test1
is then encoded as:

> test1 :: Sub1 a -> a -> Bool
> test1 d x = sub1 d x && base (super1 d) x

> class Base a where
> base :: a -> Bool
>
> class Base a => Sub1 a where
> sub1 :: a -> Bool
>
> test1 :: Sub1 a => a -> Bool
> test1 x = sub1 x && base x

Example 2 (
Program with superclasses.
).

Resolution.

Calls to functions with a qualified type generate type class constraints.
The process for checking whether these constraints can be satisfied, is known as

resolution
. For the sake of dictionary-passing elaboration, this resolution
process is augmented with the construction of the appropriate dictionary that
witnesses the satisfiability of the constraint.

2.2.
Nondeterminism and Coherence

For Haskell’98 programs there is usually only one way to construct a dictionary
for a type class constraint. Yet, in the presence of superclasses,
there may be multiple ways. Suppose we extend Example
2
with an
additional subclass and the following function:

> class Base a => Sub2 a where
> sub2 :: a -> Bool
>
> test2 :: (Sub1 a, Sub2 a) => a -> Bool
> test2 x = base x

There are two possible ways to resolve the
Base a
constraint that
arises from the call to
base
in function
test2
, resulting in
the following two translations: we can either
establish the desired constraint as the superclass of the given
Sub1 a

constraint or as the superclass of the given
Sub2 a
constraint.

> test2a, test2b :: (Sub1D a, Sub2D a) -> a -> Bool
> test2a (d1,d2) x = base (super1 d1) x
> test2b (d1,d2) x = base (super2 d2) x

Fortunately, this nondeterminism is harmless because the difference between the
two elaborations cannot be observed. Indeed, for any given type
A
,
Haskell’98 only allows a single instance
Base A
, and it does not matter whether we
access its dictionary directly or through one of its subclass instances. More
generally, this suggests that type class resolution in Haskell’98 is coherent.

If we relax the Haskell’98 non-overlap condition for locally given constraints
and adopt flexible contexts (allowing for arbitrary types in class constraints,
rather than simple type variables), another source of nondeterminism
arises. Consider:

> isZero :: Eq Int => Int -> Bool
> isZero n = n == 0

There are two ways to resolve the wanted
Eq Int
constraint that arises
from the use of
(==)
. Either we use the global
Eq Int

constraint (in
isZero1
),
or we use the locally given
Eq Int
constraint, passed as argument

d
(in
isZero2
):

> isZero1, isZero2 :: EqD Int -> Int -> Bool
> isZero1 d n = (==) eqInt n 0
> isZero2 d n = (==) d n 0

Haskell’98 does not allow the
Eq Int
constraint in
isZero
’s
signature, which overlaps with the global
Eq Int
instance; it only
allows constraints on type variables in function signatures. This prevents the
above nondeterminism in the elaboration. Yet, the nondeterminism is, once more,
harmless; there is no way that the supplied dictionary
d
can be
anything other than the global instance’s dictionary
eqInt
.
Informally, resolution remains coherent in the presence of flexible contexts.

2.3.
Contextual Difference

While it is easy to provide an informal argument for the coherence of type class
resolution, formally establishing the property is much harder.
The indirect, elaboration-based attribution of a dynamic semantics in
particular is a complicating factor, since it requires us to reason about two
languages simultaneously.
Unfortunately, there is another factor that further complicates the proof:
different elaborations of the same source program can actually be distinguished
in the target language. Consider, for instance, the target program below:

> discern :: ((Sub1D (), Sub2D ()) -> () -> Bool) -> Bool
> discern f =
> let b1 = BaseD { base = \() -> True }
> b2 = BaseD { base = \() -> False }
> d1 = Sub1D { super1 = b1 }
> d2 = Sub2D { super2 = b2 }
> in f (d1,d2) ()

We find that
discern test2a
evaluates to
True
and

discern test2b
evaluates to
False
.
Hence, since
discern
can differentiate between them,
test2a
and

test2b
clearly do not have the same meaning in the target language.

The dictionaries for
Sub1 ()
and

Sub2 ()
have different implementations for their
Base ()

superclass. The source language would never allow this, but the target language
has no notion of type classes and happily admits
discern
’s violation
of source language rules.

The problem is that the target language is more expressive than the source
language. While
test2a
and
test2b
cannot be distinguished in
any program context that arises from the source language, we can write target
programs like
discern
that are not the image of any source program and
thus do not have to play by the source language rules.

2.4.
Our Approach to Proving Coherence

To avoid the problem with contextual difference in the target language, we
employ a novel two-step approach.
We prove that any elaboration from a source language program into a
dictionary-passing encoding in the target language, can be decomposed in two
separate elaborations through an intermediate language.
We thus obtain two simpler problems for proving coherence of type class resolution.

The source language,
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{\textbf{{TC}}}}
(presented in
blue
), features full-fledged
type class resolution, and simplifies term typing with a bidirectional type
system (a technique popularized by
Pierce and Turner 2000
)
to not distract from the main objective of coherent resolution.

The intermediate language,
{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{{D}}}}
(presented in
green
), is an extension of System F that explicitly
passes type class dictionaries, and preserves the source language invariant
that there is at most one such dictionary value for any combination of class
and type. We show
{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{{D}}}}
is type-safe and strongly normalizing, and define a
logical relation that captures the contextual equivalence of two
{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{{D}}}}
terms.

The target language,
{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{\lx@text@lbrace\lx@text@rbrace}}}
(presented in
red
), is a different variant of System F
without direct support for type class dictionaries; instead it features
records, which can be used to encode dictionaries, but does not enforce
uniqueness of instances.

The different calculi are presented in Figure
1
, where the
edges denote possible elaborations.

{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{\textbf{{TC}}}}

(Fig.
2
)

{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{{D}}}}

(Fig.
8
)

{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{\lx@text@lbrace\lx@text@rbrace}}}

(Fig.
7
)

Thm.

Figure 1
.
The different calculi with elaborations

The coherence proof consists of two main parts:

Coherent Elaboration from
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{\textbf{{TC}}}}
to
{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{{D}}}}
.:

Our elaboration from
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{\textbf{{TC}}}}
into
{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{{D}}}}
is nondeterministic, but type preserving.
Furthermore, we show that any two
{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{{D}}}}
elaborations of the same
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{\textbf{{TC}}}}
term
are logically related, and prove that this logical relation implies
contextual equivalence. This establishes that the elaboration from
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{\textbf{{TC}}}}
to

{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{{D}}}}
is coherent.

Deterministic Elaboration from
{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{{D}}}}
to
{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{\lx@text@lbrace\lx@text@rbrace}}}
.:

Because of the syntactic similarity between
{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{{D}}}}
and

{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{\lx@text@lbrace\lx@text@rbrace}}}
, the elaboration from the former into the latter is a more
straightforward affair. In addition to being type preserving, it is also
deterministic, and preserves contextual equivalence.

These results are easily combined to show the coherence of the elaboration
from
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{\textbf{{TC}}}}
to
{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{\lx@text@lbrace\lx@text@rbrace}}}
, which implies coherence of elaboration-based type
class resolution.
The full proofs can be found in the appendix. Note that the proofs depend on a
number of standard boilerplate conjectures (e.g., substitution lemmas), which can be
found in Sections
J.1
and
K.1
of the appendix.

3.
Source Language
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{\textbf{{TC}}}}

This section presents our source language
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{\textbf{{TC}}}}
, a basic calculus which
isolates nondeterministic resolution.
The calculus only supports features that are
essential for type class resolution and its coherence.

Consequently, the language is strongly normalizing, and thus does not support
recursive let expressions, mutual recursion or recursive methods.
This is a sensible choice, as recursion does not affect the fundamentals of the
coherence proof.
This work could include recursion through step
indexing
(
Ahmed 2006
)
, a well-known technique,
but this would significantly clutter the proof.
Recursion is discussed in more detail in Section
8
.

Furthermore, two notable design decisions were made in the support of
superclasses in
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{\textbf{{TC}}}}
.
Firstly, similar to GHC,
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{\textbf{{TC}}}}
derives all possible superclass constraints
from their subclass constraints in advance, instead of deriving them
“just-in-time” during resolution. The advantage of this approach is that it
streamlines the actual resolution process.

Secondly, similar to Coq
(
Sozeau and Oury 2008
)
and unlike
Wadler and Blott 1989
, we pass superclass
dictionaries alongside their subclass dictionaries, i.e., in a
flattened

form, instead of nesting them inside their subclass dictionaries.
As it is not too difficult to see that both approaches are isomorphic,
flattening the superclasses does not impact the coherence of resolution.
It does, however, considerably simplify the
proof, since this way neither our type class
resolution mechanism, nor the intermediate language
{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{{D}}}}

(Section
6
) need to have any
support for superclasses and can treat them as regular local constraints.
A more structured representation would give rise to additional complexity, but
would not alter the essence of the proof.

Syntax.

Figure
2
presents the, mostly
standard, syntax.
Programs consist of a number of class (with superclasses) and instance
declarations, and an expression.
For the sake of simplicity and well-foundedness, the declarations are ordered
and can only refer to previous declarations.

.
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{\textbf{{TC}}}}
syntax

Following
Jones 1994
’s qualified types framework, we distinguish between three
sorts of types: monotypes
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\tau}}}
, qualified types
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\rho}}}
which include
constraints, and type schemes
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\sigma}}}
which include type abstractions.
Constraints differentiate between full constraint schemes
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{C}}}

and simple class constraints
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{Q}}}
. Observe that we allow flexible contexts
in the qualified types; they are not restricted to constraints on type variables.

The definition of expressions
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{e}}}
is standard, but with a few notable exceptions.
Firstly, the language differentiates syntactically between regular
variables
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{x}}}
and method names
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{m}}}
, which are introduced
in class declarations.
Secondly, type annotations
\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{e}}}::{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\tau}}}}}
allow the programmer to manually
assign a monotype to an expression. This is useful for resolving ambiguity—see
the
Typing
paragraph below.
Finally, let bindings include type annotations with a type scheme
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\sigma}}}
,
allowing the programmer to introduce local constraints—also discussed
in the
Typing
paragraph.
Note that we use Haskell syntax for class and instance declarations.

There are three
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{\textbf{{TC}}}}
environments: two global ones and one local
environment.
Firstly, the global class environment
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}
stores all class declarations.
Each entry in
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}
contains the method name
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{m}}}
, any superclasses
\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\overline{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\mathit{TC}_{i}\penalty\ a}}}}}
, the
class
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\mathit{TC}}}}\,{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{a}}}
itself and the corresponding method type
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\sigma}}}
.

Secondly, the global program context
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{P}}}
contains all instance declarations.
Each entry in
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{P}}}
consists of a unique dictionary constructor
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{D}}}
, its corresponding
constraint
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{C}}}
, the method name
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{m}}}
and its implementation

{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{e}}}
, together with the context
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma}}}
under which
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{e}}}
should be
interpreted. This context contains the local axioms available in this
instance declaration, as well as any axioms which explicitly annotate the method
type signature.

Thirdly, the local typing environment
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma}}}
, besides containing the
default term and type variables
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{x}}}
and
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{a}}}
, also stores any local
axioms
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{Q}}}
. As opposed to the program context
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{P}}}
,

{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma}}}
does not contain any type class instances. Instead, the (local) axioms
are associated with a dictionary variable
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\delta}}}
.
Sections
6
and
6.1
explain the use of these dictionaries.

Typing.

Our type system features two design choices to
eliminate the possibility of ambiguous type schemes.
This allows us to focus on the coherence of type class
resolution, by making our proof orthogonal to ambiguous type schemes, the source
of ambiguity which has already been studied by
Jones 1993
.
We thus side-step an already solved problem and focus on tackling the full
problem of resolution coherence.

Firstly, we require type signatures to be unambiguous
(Figure
4
, right-hand side)
to make sure that all newly introduced type variables
are bound in the head of the type (the remaining monotype after dropping all type
and constraint abstractions).
This prevents ambiguous expressions such as:

> let f : forall a . Eq a => Int -> Int -- ambiguous
> = \ x . x + 1 in f 42

Secondly, we use a bidirectional type system rather than
a fully declarative one. A bidirectional type system distinguishes between two
typing modes:
inference
and
check
mode.
The former synthesizes a type from the given expression, while the latter checks
whether a given expression is of a given type.
Special in our setting is that
variables can only be typed in check mode, to ensure that only a single
instantiation exists.
This avoids the ambiguity that can arise when instantiating type
variables in inference mode.
Consider the following example:

> let y : forall a . Eq a => a -> a = ...
> in const 1 y

where
const x
is the constant function, which evaluates to
x

for any input.
The instantiation of
y
’s type scheme is not uniquely determined by the
context in which it is used. In a declarative type system or in inference mode,
this ambiguity would result in multiple distinct typings and corresponding
elaborations. While this ambiguity is harmless, it is not the focus of this
work. Hence, to focus exclusively on the resolution, we use a bidirectional type
system with check mode for variables to eliminate this irrelevant source of ambiguity.

}\,{\overline{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{Q}}}}_{\mathit{p}}\Rightarrow{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\mathit{TC}}}}\,{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\tau}}}\,\textbf{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{where}} }\,\{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{m}}}={\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{e}}}\}}}:\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{D}}}:\forall{\overline{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{b}}}}_{\mathit{k}}.{\overline{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{Q}}}}_{\mathit{q}}\Rightarrow{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\mathit{TC}}}}\,{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\tau}}}).{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{m}}}\mapsto{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma}}}^{\prime}:{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{e}}}}}}\quad\textsc{right=\scriptsize{{sInstT-inst}}}}

Figure 6
.
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{\textbf{{TC}}}}
instance declaration typing

Through a let binding (rule
sTm-infT-let
), the programmer provides a
type scheme for a variable, thus potentially introducing local constraints.
As explained above, the unambiguity check from
Figure
4
(right-hand side) requires the
provided type scheme to be unambiguous.
In order to flatten the superclasses, the rule takes the closure
over the superclass relation (left-hand side of Figure
4
) of the
user provided constraints
\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\overline{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{Q}}}}_{\mathit{i}}}}
. It then adds the resulting set of constraints

\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\overline{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{Q}}}}_{\mathit{k}}}}
to the typing environment, under which to typecheck
\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{e}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}}
.
Finally, the type of
\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{e}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}}
is inferred under the extended environment.

Rule
sTm-checkT-meth
types a method call
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{m}}}
in
check mode, like regular variables, to avoid any ambiguity in the instantiation of the type variables in
the method’s type scheme.
This includes both the type variable
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{a}}}
from the class and any
additional free variables
\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\overline{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{a}}}}_{\mathit{j}}}}
in the method type.
Furthermore, the rules uses the unambig-relation to avoid ambiguity in the
method type scheme itself, by requiring that both sets
of type variables have to occur in the head of the method type.
The rule also checks that all required constraints

\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\overline{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{Q}}}}_{\mathit{i}}}}
from the method type can be
entailed.

The instance typing rule can be found in
Figure
6
. The relation

\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{P}}}}};\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}}\vdash_{inst}\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{inst}}}}}:\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{P}}}^{\prime}}}
denotes that an instance declaration

{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{inst}}}
results in a
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{\textbf{{TC}}}}
program context
\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{P}}}^{\prime}}}
,
while being typed under environments
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{P}}}
and
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}
.
The unambig-relation for constraints
(Figure
4
, bottom right),
similarly to the unambig-relation for types,
checks that all free type variables
\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\overline{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{b}}}}_{\mathit{k}}}}
in the instance context
occur in the instance type
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\tau}}}
as well, in order to avoid ambiguity.
Like in the
sTm-infT-let
rule explained above, the
superclasses of the instance context
\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\overline{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{Q}}}}_{\mathit{p}}}}
are flattened into additional local
constraints
\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\overline{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{Q}}}}_{\mathit{q}}}}
and added to the environment.
The superclasses
\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\overline{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{Q}}}}^{\prime}_{\mathit{i}}}}
of the instantiated type
class are then checked to be entailed under this extended environment.
The rule checks that no overlapping instance declarations
\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{D}}}^{\prime}}}
have been defined.
Finally, the program context is extended with the new instance axiom
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{D}}}
, consisting
of a constraint scheme that requires the full set of local constraints
\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\overline{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{Q}}}}_{\mathit{q}}}}
.

Type Class Resolution.

The type class resolution rules can be found in
Figure
5
, where

\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{P}}}}};\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma}}}}}\vDash\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{Q}}}}}
denotes that a class constraint
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{Q}}}

is entailed under the environments
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{P}}}
,
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}
and
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma}}}
.
A wanted constraint
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{Q}}}
can either be resolved
using a locally available constraint
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\delta}}}
(
sEntailT-local
) or through a
global instance declaration
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{D}}}

(
sEntailT-inst
).

The former is entirely straightforward. The latter is more involved as
an instance
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{D}}}
may have an instance context
\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\overline{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{Q}}}}^{\prime}_{\mathit{i}}}}
, which has to be
recursively resolved. Before resolving the context, the type variables

\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\overline{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{a}}}}_{\mathit{j}}}}
are instantiated with the
corresponding concrete types
\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\overline{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\tau}}}}_{\mathit{j}}}}
, originating from the wanted
constraint
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{Q}}}
.

Note that the type class resolution mechanism does not require any specific
support for superclasses, as these have all been flattened into regular local
constraints.

4.
Target Language
{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{\lx@text@lbrace\lx@text@rbrace}}}

This section covers our target language
{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{\lx@text@lbrace\lx@text@rbrace}}}
, and the elaboration from

{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{\textbf{{TC}}}}
to
{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{\lx@text@lbrace\lx@text@rbrace}}}
.

The target language is System F with records, which we consider a
reasonable subcalculus of those used by
Haskell compilers. Its syntax is shown in Figure
7
.
We omit its standard typing rules and call-by-name operational semantics and refer the reader
to
Pierce 2002
, or Section
E
of the appendix.

Figure 7
.
Target language syntax

4.1.
Elaboration from
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{\textbf{{TC}}}}
to
{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{\lx@text@lbrace\lx@text@rbrace}}}

The red aspects in Figure
3
denote the elaboration of

{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{\textbf{{TC}}}}
terms to
{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{\lx@text@lbrace\lx@text@rbrace}}}
. We have adopted the convention
that any red
{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{\lx@text@lbrace\lx@text@rbrace}}}
types are the elaborated forms of their
identically named blue
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{\textbf{{TC}}}}
counterparts.
This elaboration maps most
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{\textbf{{TC}}}}
forms on identical
{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{\lx@text@lbrace\lx@text@rbrace}}}
terms,
with the exception of a few notable cases:

(a)

The interesting aspect of elaborating let expressions
(
sTm-infT-let
) is that, as mentioned previously, superclasses are
flattened into additional local constraints.
The elaborated expression thus explicitly requires both the type
variables and the full closure of the local constraints.

(b)

As opposed to
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{\textbf{{TC}}}}
, dictionary and type application are made explicit in

{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{\lx@text@lbrace\lx@text@rbrace}}}
. When elaborating variables
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{x}}}
and method references

{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{m}}}
(
sTm-checkT-meth
), all previously substituted types

\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\overline{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\tau}}}}_{\mathit{j}}}}
are now explicitly applied, together with the dictionary expressions
\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\overline{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{e}}}}_{\mathit{i}}}}
.
Furthermore, method names
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{m}}}
are elaborated to
{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{\lx@text@lbrace\lx@text@rbrace}}}
record
labels
{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{m}}}
and therefore cannot appear by themselves, but must be
applied to a record expression
{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{e}}}
, which originates from resolving the
class constraint.

Type class resolution (Figure
5
) of a
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{\textbf{{TC}}}}

constraint
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{Q}}}
results in a
{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{\lx@text@lbrace\lx@text@rbrace}}}
expression
{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{e}}}
.
When resolving the wanted constraint using a locally available constraint
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\delta}}}

(
sEntailT-local
), this results in a regular term variable
{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{\delta}}}

(which keeps the name of its
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{\textbf{{TC}}}}
counterpart for readability).
On the other hand, when resolving with the use of a global instance declaration
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{D}}}
(
sEntailT-inst
), a record
expression is constructed, containing the method name
{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{m}}}
and its corresponding
implementation
{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{e}}}
. This method implementation now explicitly abstracts over the
type variables
\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\overline{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{b}}}}_{\mathit{k}}}}
and term variables
\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\overline{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{\delta}}}}_{\mathit{h}}}}

originating from the method types’s class constraints
\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\overline{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{Q}}}}_{\mathit{h}}}}
, which
annotate the class declaration.
Furthermore, the record expression is nested in abstractions
over the type variables
\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\overline{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{a}}}}_{\mathit{j}}}}
and term variables
\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\overline{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{\delta}}}}^{\prime}_{\mathit{i}}}}
arising from the corresponding instance
constraints
\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\overline{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{Q}}}}^{\prime}_{\mathit{i}}}}
.
These abstractions are immediately instantiated by applying

(a)

the types
\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\overline{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{\sigma}}}}_{\mathit{j}}}}
needed for matching the wanted constraint
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{Q}}}
to the instance
declaration
\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{Q}}}^{\prime}}}
and

(b)

the expressions
\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\overline{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{e}}}}_{\mathit{i}}}}
constructed by resolving the
instance context constraints
\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\overline{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{Q}}}}^{\prime}_{\mathit{i}}}}
.

Example
1

{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{\textbf{{TC}}}}
to
{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{\lx@text@lbrace\lx@text@rbrace}}}
.

Typing the Example
1
program results in the following
environments:

\displaystyle\qquad{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{P}}}=\penalty\

\displaystyle\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{D}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}:{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{Eq}}}\,{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{Int}}}).{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{(==)}}}\mapsto\bullet:{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{primEqInt}}}}}

\displaystyle\quad\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\lambda({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{x}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}},{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{y}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}).\lambda({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{x}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}},{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{y}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}).\penalty\ {\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{(\&\&)}}}\,({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{(==)}}}\,{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{x}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}\,{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{x}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}})\,({\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{(==)}}}\,{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{y}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}\,{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{y}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}})}}

The
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{Eq}}}
class straightforwardly gets stored in the class environment

{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}
. Instances are stored in the
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{\textbf{{TC}}}}
program context
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{P}}}

(containing the dictionary constructor, the corresponding constraint, the method
implementation and the environment under which to interpret this expression).
Storing the instance declaration for
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{Eq}}}\,{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{Int}}}
is
clear-cut. The instance for tuples on the other hand is somewhat more complex, since it
requires an instance context, containing the local constraints
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{Eq}}}\,{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{a}}}
and

{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{Eq}}}\,{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{b}}}
. These constraints are made explicit, that is, the
corresponding dictionaries are required by the elaborated
implementation.

Elaborating the
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{\textbf{{TC}}}}
expression results in the following
{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{\lx@text@lbrace\lx@text@rbrace}}}

expression:

&\quad\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{Int}}}\,{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{Int}}}\,\{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{(==)}}}={\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{primEqInt}}}\}\,\{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{(==)}}}={\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{primEqInt}}}\}\,(5,42)\,}}\end{aligned}

\displaystyle\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{\textbf{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{in}} }\,{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{main}}}}}

Note that the
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{Eq}}}\,{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{a}}}
constraint is made explicit in the implementation
of
{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{\mathit{refl}}}}
, by abstracting over the constraint
(elaborated to
{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{\lx@text@lbrace\lx@text@rbrace}}}
as the record type

\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{\{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{(==)}}}:{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{a}}}\rightarrow{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{a}}}\rightarrow\mathit{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{Bool}}}\}}}
, which stores the method name and its
corresponding type)
with the use of the record variable
\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{\delta}}}_{{\mathrm{3}}}}}
.
When this function is called in
{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{main}}}
, both the type and the
dictionary variable are instantiated. The latter is performed by (recursively) constructing a
dictionary expression, using the type class resolution mechanism, as explained
above in Section
4.1
.

Example

{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{\textbf{{TC}}}}

{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{\lx@text@lbrace\lx@text@rbrace}}}
expression:

\displaystyle\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{\textbf{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{let}} }\,{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{test}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}}\begin{aligned} &\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{:\forall{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{a}}}.\{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{base}}}:{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{a}}}\rightarrow\mathit{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{Bool}}}\}\rightarrow\{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{sub}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}:{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{a}}}\rightarrow\mathit{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{Bool}}}\}}}\\
&\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{\quad\rightarrow\{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{base}}}:{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{a}}}\rightarrow\mathit{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{Bool}}}\}\rightarrow\{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{sub}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}:{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{a}}}\rightarrow\mathit{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{Bool}}}\}\rightarrow{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{a}}}\rightarrow\mathit{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{Bool}}}}}\\
&\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{=\Lambda{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{a}}}.\lambda{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{\delta}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}:\{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{base}}}:{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{a}}}\rightarrow\mathit{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{Bool}}}\}.\lambda{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{\delta}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}:\{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{sub}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}:{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{a}}}\rightarrow\mathit{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{Bool}}}\}.}}\\
&\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{\quad\lambda{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{\delta}}}_{{\mathrm{3}}}:\{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{base}}}:{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{a}}}\rightarrow\mathit{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{Bool}}}\}.\lambda{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{\delta}}}_{{\mathrm{4}}}:\{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{sub}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}:{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{a}}}\rightarrow\mathit{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{Bool}}}\}.\lambda{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{x}}}:{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{a}}}.\penalty\ {\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{\delta}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}.{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{base}}}\,{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{x}}}\,}}\\
\end{aligned}

\displaystyle\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{\textbf{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{in}} }\,\mathit{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{True}}}}}

Note that the
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{\textbf{{TC}}}}
expression requires two local constraints:

\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{Sub}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}\,{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{a}}}}}
and
\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{Sub}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}\,{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{a}}}}}
.
However, after flattening the superclasses and adding them to the local
constraints, the elaborated
{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{\lx@text@lbrace\lx@text@rbrace}}}
expression requires (the elaborated form
of) the

\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{Base}}}\,{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{a}}}}}
,
\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{Sub}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}\,{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{a}}}}}
,
\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{Base}}}\,{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{a}}}}}
and

\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{Sub}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}\,{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{a}}}}}
constraints. Notice the duplicate
\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{Base}}}\,{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{a}}}}}
entry.
Either of these two entries can be used for calling
the method
{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{base}}}
.
We have arbitrarily selected the first here.
The next section proves that both options are equivalent
and can be used interchangeably.

5.
Coherence

This section provides an outline for our coherence proof, and defines the
required notions.
We first provide a definition of

contextual equivalence

(
Morris Jr 1969
)
, which captures that
two expressions have the same meaning.

5.1.
Contextual Equivalence

In order to formally discuss the concept of contextual equivalence, we first define the notion of an

expression context
.

Expression Contexts.

An expression context
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{M}}}
is an expression
with a single hole, for which another expression
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{e}}}
can be filled in,
denoted as
\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{M}}}[{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{e}}}]}}
.
The syntax can be found in Figure
2
.

The typing judgment for an expression context
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{M}}}
is of the form

\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{M}}}}}:(\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{P}}}}};\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma}}}}}\Rightarrow\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\tau}}}}})\mapsto(\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{P}}}}};\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma}}}^{\prime}}}\Rightarrow\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\tau}}}^{\prime}}})\rightsquigarrow\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{M}}}}}
.
This means that for any
expression
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{e}}}
such that
\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{P}}}}};\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma}}}}}\vdash_{tm}\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{e}}}}}\Rightarrow\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\tau}}}}}{\rightsquigarrow\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{e}}}}}}
,
we have
\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{P}}}}};\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma}}}^{\prime}}}\vdash_{tm}\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{M}}}[{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{e}}}]}}\Rightarrow\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\tau}}}^{\prime}}}{\rightsquigarrow\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{e}}}^{\prime}}}}
.
Following regular
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{\textbf{{TC}}}}
term typing, context typing spans all combinations
of type inference and checking mode:

\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{M}}}}}:(\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{P}}}}};\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma}}}}}\Rightarrow\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\tau}}}}})\mapsto(\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{P}}}}};\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma}}}^{\prime}}}\Leftarrow\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\tau}}}^{\prime}}})\rightsquigarrow\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{M}}}}}
,

\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{M}}}}}:(\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{P}}}}};\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma}}}}}\Leftarrow\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\tau}}}}})\mapsto(\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{P}}}}};\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma}}}^{\prime}}}\Rightarrow\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\tau}}}^{\prime}}})\rightsquigarrow\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{M}}}}}
and

\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{M}}}}}:(\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{P}}}}};\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma}}}}}\Leftarrow\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\tau}}}}})\mapsto(\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{P}}}}};\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma}}}^{\prime}}}\Leftarrow\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\tau}}}^{\prime}}})\rightsquigarrow\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{M}}}}}
.

For example, the simplest expression context is the
empty context
\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{[\,\bullet\,]}}:(\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{P}}}}};\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma}}}}}\Rightarrow\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\tau}}}}})\mapsto(\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{P}}}}};\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma}}}}}\Rightarrow\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\tau}}}}})\rightsquigarrow\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{[\,\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{\bullet}}\,]}}
.

Now we can formally define contextual equivalence. Note that the small step
operational semantics can be found in Section
E.4
of the appendix.
The environment and type well-formedness judgments can be found in
Sections
B.4
and
B.1
of the appendix respectively.

Definition 0 (Kleene Equivalence).

Two
{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{\lx@text@lbrace\lx@text@rbrace}}}
expressions
\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{e}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}}
and
\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{e}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}}
are
Kleene equivalent, written
\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{e}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}}\simeq\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{e}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}}
,

if there exists
a value
{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{v}}}
such that
\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{e}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}}\longrightarrow^{*}\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{v}}}}}
, and
\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{e}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}}\longrightarrow^{*}\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{v}}}}}
.

Definition 0 (Contextual Equivalence).

Two expressions
\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{\Gamma}}}}}\vdash_{tm}\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{e}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}}:\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{\sigma}}}}}
and
\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{\Gamma}}}}}\vdash_{tm}\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{e}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}}:\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{\sigma}}}}}
,

where
\vdash_{ctx}\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{P}}}}};\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma}}}}}\rightsquigarrow\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{\Gamma}}}}}
and
\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma}}}}}\vdash_{ty}\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\tau}}}}}\,{{\rightsquigarrow\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{\sigma}}}}}}}
,

are contextually equivalent, written
\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{P}}}}};\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma}}}}}\vdash\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{e}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}}\simeq_{ctx}\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{e}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}}:\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\tau}}}}}
,

if forall
\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{M}}}}}:(\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{P}}}}};\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma}}}}}\Rightarrow\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\tau}}}}})\mapsto(\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{P}}}}};\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\bullet}}\Rightarrow\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\mathit{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{Bool}}}}})\rightsquigarrow\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{M}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}}

and
\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{M}}}}}:(\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{P}}}}};\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma}}}}}\Rightarrow\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\tau}}}}})\mapsto(\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{P}}}}};\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\bullet}}\Rightarrow\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\mathit{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{Bool}}}}})\rightsquigarrow\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{M}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}}

implies
\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{M}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}[{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{e}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}]}}\simeq\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{M}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}[{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{e}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}]}}
.

The definition is adapted from
Harper 2016
.
Intuitively, contextual equivalence means that two open expressions are
observationally indistinguishable, when used in any program that instantiates
the expressions’ free variables.

5.2.
Coherence

We can now make a first attempt to prove
that different translations of the same
source program are contextually equivalent. The program typing judgment
can be found in Section
B.2
of the appendix.

Theorem 3 (Coherence).

If
\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\bullet}};\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\bullet}}\vdash_{pgm}\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{pgm}}}}}:\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\tau}}}}};\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{P}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}};\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}}\rightsquigarrow\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{e}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}}
and
\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\bullet}};\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\bullet}}\vdash_{pgm}\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{pgm}}}}}:\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\tau}}}}};\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{P}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}};\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}}\rightsquigarrow\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{e}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}}

then
\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}}=\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}}
,
\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{P}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}}=\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{P}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}}
and
\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{P}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}};\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}};\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\bullet}}\vdash\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{e}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}}\simeq_{ctx}\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{e}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}}:\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\tau}}}}}
.

We first set out to prove the simpler variant, which only considers
expressions
2

Theorem
4
also has a type checking mode
counterpart, which has been omitted here for space reasons.
.

Theorem 4 (Expression Coherence).

If
\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{P}}}}};\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma}}}}}\vdash_{tm}\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{e}}}}}\Rightarrow\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\tau}}}}}{\rightsquigarrow\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{e}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}}}
and
\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{P}}}}};\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma}}}}}\vdash_{tm}\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{e}}}}}\Rightarrow\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\tau}}}}}{\rightsquigarrow\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{e}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}}}

then
\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{P}}}}};\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma}}}}}\vdash\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{e}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}}\simeq_{ctx}\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{e}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}}:\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\tau}}}}}
.

The main requirement which makes type class resolution coherent is that type
class instances do not overlap. However, since
{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{\lx@text@lbrace\lx@text@rbrace}}}
uses records to encode
dictionaries, the
{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{\lx@text@lbrace\lx@text@rbrace}}}
language does not enforce this crucial uniqueness property.
In order to prove Theorem
3
, we introduce an
additional intermediate language
{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{{D}}}}
, which captures the invariant that
type class instances do not overlap, and makes it explicit.

6.
Intermediate Language
{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{{D}}}}

This section presents our intermediate language
{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{{D}}}}
.
The language is modeled with three main goals in mind:

(a)

{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{{D}}}}
should explicitly pass type class dictionaries, which are
implicit in
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{\textbf{{TC}}}}
;

(b)

the
{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{{D}}}}
type system should capture the uniqueness of
dictionaries, thus enforcing the elaboration from

{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{\textbf{{TC}}}}
to preserve full abstraction; and

(c)

{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{{D}}}}
expressions should elaborate straightforwardly and
deterministically to the target language
{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{\lx@text@lbrace\lx@text@rbrace}}}
(System F with records, see
Section
4
).

To this end,
{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{{D}}}}
is an extension of System F, with built-in support for
dictionaries. These dictionaries differ from those commonly used in
Haskell compilers in that they are special constants rather than a record of
method implementations. A separate global map
{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}
from dictionaries
to method implementations gives access to the latter. Note that this setup does
not allow programs to introduce new (and possibly overlapping) dictionaries dynamically.
All dictionaries have to be provided upfront, where uniqueness is easily enforced.

Syntax.

Figure
8
shows selected syntax of
{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{{D}}}}
;
the basic System F constructs are omitted and can be found in
Section
A.2
of the appendix.

Figure 8
.
{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{{D}}}}
, selected syntax

{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{{D}}}}
introduces a new syntactic sort of
dictionaries
{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{d}}}
that can either be a dictionary variable

{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\delta}}}
or a dictionary constructor
{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{D}}}
. A dictionary
constructor has a number (possibly zero) of type and dictionary parameters and always
appears in fully-applied form.
Each constructor corresponds to a unique instance declaration, and is
mapped to its method implementation by the global environment
{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}
.

Expressions have explicit application and abstraction forms for dictionaries.
Furthermore, similarly to
{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{\lx@text@lbrace\lx@text@rbrace}}}
, method names can no longer
be used on their own. Instead, they have to be applied explicitly to a
dictionary, in the form
{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{d}}}.{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{m}}}
.

{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{{D}}}}
types
{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\sigma}}}
or
{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\tau}}}
are identical to the well-known
System F types, with the addition of a special function type
\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{Q}}}\Rightarrow{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\sigma}}}}}

for dictionary abstractions.

Similarly to
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{\textbf{{TC}}}}
,
{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{{D}}}}
features two global
and a single local environment
{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma}}}
. The latter is similar to the
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{\textbf{{TC}}}}

typing environment
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma}}}
. However, there are notable differences between
the global environments. The
{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{{D}}}}
class environment
{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}

does not contain any superclass information.
The reason for this is that, as previously mentioned in Section
3
,
superclass constraints in the source language
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{\textbf{{TC}}}}
are flattened into local
constraints, and stored in the typing environment
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma}}}
.
The analog to the
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{\textbf{{TC}}}}
program context

{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{P}}}
is the
{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{{D}}}}
method environment
{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}
, storing
information about all dictionary constructors
{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{D}}}
.
Each constructor corresponds to a unique instance declaration,
and stores the accompanying method implementations.

Typing.

Figure
9
(left-hand side) shows selected typing rules for

{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{{D}}}}
expressions.
The red parts can be safely ignored
for now, as they will be explained in detail in Section
6.2
.
The judgment
\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma}}}}}\vdash_{tm}\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{e}}}}}:\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\sigma}}}}}
expresses that the
{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{{D}}}}

term
{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{e}}}
of type
{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\sigma}}}
is well-typed under environments
{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}
,

{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}
and
{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma}}}
.
As shown by rule
iTm-method
, the type of a method variable applied to a
dictionary is simply the corresponding method type (as stored in the
static class environment), where the type variable has been substituted for the
corresponding dictionary type.

\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma}}}}}\vdash_{tm}\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{e}}}}}:\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\sigma}}}}}\rightsquigarrow\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{e}}}}}
