Two expressions
\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma}}}}}\vdash_{tm}\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{e}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}}:\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\sigma}}}}}
and
\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma}}}}}\vdash_{tm}\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{e}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}}:\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\sigma}}}}}
,

are contextually equivalent, written

\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma}}}}}\vdash\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}}:\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{e}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}}\simeq_{ctx}\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}}:\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{e}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}}:\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\sigma}}}}}
,

if forall
\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{M}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}}:(\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma}}}}}\Rightarrow\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\sigma}}}}})\mapsto(\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\bullet}}\Rightarrow\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\mathit{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{Bool}}}}})

and forall
\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{M}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}}:(\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma}}}}}\Rightarrow\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\sigma}}}}})\mapsto(\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\bullet}}\Rightarrow\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\mathit{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{Bool}}}}})

where
\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}}:\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{M}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}}\simeq_{log}\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}}:\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{M}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}}:(\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma}}}}}\Rightarrow\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\sigma}}}}})\mapsto(\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\bullet}}\Rightarrow\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\mathit{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{Bool}}}}})
,

we have that
\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}}:\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{M}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}[{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{e}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}]}}\simeq\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}}:\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{M}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}[{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{e}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}]}}
.

Theorem 11 (Logical Equivalence implies Contextual Equivalence).

If
\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma}}}}}\vdash\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}}:\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{e}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}}\simeq_{log}\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}}:\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{e}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}}:\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\sigma}}}}}
then
\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma}}}}}\vdash\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}}:\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{e}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}}\simeq_{ctx}\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}}:\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{e}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}}:\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\sigma}}}}}
.

7.2.
Deterministic Elaboration from
{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{{D}}}}
to
{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{\lx@text@lbrace\lx@text@rbrace}}}

7.2.1.
Contextual Equivalence.

Similarly to expressions, the elaboration from a
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{\textbf{{TC}}}}
context
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{M}}}
to a

{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{\lx@text@lbrace\lx@text@rbrace}}}
context
{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{M}}}
can always be decomposed into two elaborations,
through a
{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{{D}}}}
context
{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{M}}}
.
The syntax and typing judgments can be found in Sections
A
and
F
of
the appendix, respectively.

We now formally define contextual equivalence for
{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{\lx@text@lbrace\lx@text@rbrace}}}
expressions through

{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{{D}}}}
contexts.

Definition 0 (Contextual Equivalence in
{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{{D}}}}
Context).

Two expressions
\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{\Gamma}}}}}\vdash_{tm}\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{e}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}}:\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{\sigma}}}}}
and
\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{\Gamma}}}}}\vdash_{tm}\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{e}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}}:\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{\sigma}}}}}
,

where
\vdash_{ctx}\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{P}}}}};\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma}}}}}\rightsquigarrow\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{\Gamma}}}}}
and
\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma}}}}}\vdash_{ty}\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\tau}}}}}\,{{\rightsquigarrow\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{\sigma}}}}}}}
,

are contextually equivalent, written
\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma}}}}}\vdash\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}}:\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{e}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}}\simeq_{ctx}\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}}:\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{e}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}}:\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\sigma}}}}}
,

if forall
\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{M}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}}:(\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma}}}}}\Rightarrow\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\sigma}}}}})\mapsto(\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\bullet}}\Rightarrow\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\mathit{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{Bool}}}}}){\rightsquigarrow\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{M}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}}}

and forall
\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{M}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}}:(\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma}}}}}\Rightarrow\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\sigma}}}}})\mapsto(\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\bullet}}\Rightarrow\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\mathit{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{Bool}}}}}){\rightsquigarrow\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{M}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}}}

where
\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}}:\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{M}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}}\simeq_{log}\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}}:\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{M}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}}:(\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma}}}}}\Rightarrow\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\sigma}}}}})\mapsto(\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\bullet}}\Rightarrow\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\mathit{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{Bool}}}}})
,

we have that
\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{M}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}[{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{e}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}]}}\simeq\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{M}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}[{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{e}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}]}}
,

where
\vdash_{ctx}^{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{M}}}\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{P}}}}};\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma}}}}}\rightsquigarrow\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma}}}}}
and
\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma}}}}}\rightsquigarrow\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{\Gamma}}}}}
and
\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma}}}}}\vdash_{ty}^{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{M}}}\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\tau}}}}}\,{{\rightsquigarrow\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\sigma}}}}}}}
and
\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma}}}}}\vdash_{ty}\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\sigma}}}}}{\rightsquigarrow\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{\sigma}}}}}}
.

7.2.2.
Proof of
{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{{D}}}}
-to-
{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{\lx@text@lbrace\lx@text@rbrace}}}
Coherence.

We continue by proving that contextual equivalence is preserved by the
elaboration from
{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{{D}}}}
to
{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{\lx@text@lbrace\lx@text@rbrace}}}
:

Theorem 13 (Elaboration preserves Contextual Equivalence).

If
\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma}}}}}\vdash\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}}:\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{e}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}}\simeq_{ctx}\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}}:\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{e}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}}:\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\sigma}}}}}

and
\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma}}}}}\vdash_{tm}\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{e}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}}:\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\sigma}}}}}{\rightsquigarrow\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{e}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}}}
and
\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma}}}}}\vdash_{tm}\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{e}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}}:\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\sigma}}}}}{\rightsquigarrow\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{e}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}}}
and
\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma}}}}}\rightsquigarrow\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{\Gamma}}}}}

then
\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma}}}}}\vdash\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}}:\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{e}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}}\simeq_{ctx}\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}}:\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{e}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}}:\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\sigma}}}}}
.

7.2.3.
Proof of
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{\textbf{{TC}}}}
-to-
{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{\lx@text@lbrace\lx@text@rbrace}}}
Coherence.

Finally, in order to link back to Theorem
4
(which has no notion of

{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{{D}}}}
), we prove that contextual equivalence with
{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{{D}}}}
contexts implies
contextual equivalence with
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{\textbf{{TC}}}}
contexts:

Theorem 14 (Contextual Equivalence in
{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{{D}}}}
implies Contextual
Equivalence in
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{\textbf{{TC}}}}
).

If
\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma}}}}}\vdash\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}}:\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{e}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}}\simeq_{ctx}\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}}:\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{e}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}}:\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\sigma}}}}}

and
\vdash_{ctx}^{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{M}}}\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{P}}}}};\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma}}}}}\rightsquigarrow\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma}}}}}
and
\vdash_{ctx}^{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{M}}}\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{P}}}}};\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma}}}}}\rightsquigarrow\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma}}}}}
and
\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma}}}}}\vdash_{ty}^{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{M}}}\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\tau}}}}}\,{{\rightsquigarrow\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\sigma}}}}}}}

then
\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{P}}}}};\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma}}}}}\vdash\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{e}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}}\simeq_{ctx}\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{e}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}}:\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\tau}}}}}
.

For clarity, we restate coherence Theorems

8.
Discussion of Possible Extensions

As the goal of this work was to find a proof technique to formally establish
coherence for type class resolution,
a stripped down source calculus was employed in order not to clutter the proof.
This section provides a brief discussion of extending our
coherence proof to support several mainstream language features.

Ambiguous Type Schemes.

As mentioned previously, our work is
orthogonal to ambiguous type schemes, which have already been extensively studied
by
Jones 1993
. We believe our work and the proof by Jones can be combined,
which would then relax the restriction of bidirectional type checking, and prove
coherence for both ambiguous type schemes and type class resolution.

General Recursion.

Recursion is an important feature, present in any real world programming
language.
It is important to note that, while
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}\boldsymbol{\lambda}_{\textbf{{TC}}}}
does not feature recursion on
the expression level (as it does not affect the essence of the coherence proof),
type class resolution itself is recursive.
Dictionary values are constructed dynamically from a statically given set of
dictionary constructors (one constructor per type class instance). The system
can thus recursively generate an arbitrary number of dictionaries from a finite
set of instances.

Our logical relations can be adapted to support general recursion, through
well-known techniques, such as step indexing
(
Ahmed 2006
)
.
While this results in a
significantly longer and more cluttered proof, we do not anticipate any
major complications.

Multi-Parameter Type Classes.

Just like regular type class instances, multi-parameter instances (as supported
by GHC) are subject to
the no-overlap rule. Hence, they respect our main assumption. They may indeed
give rise to more ambiguity, but this is the kind of ambiguity that is studied
by
Jones 1993
, not the kind that shows up during resolution.
Note that functional dependencies were originally introduced
by
Jones 2000
as a way to resolve the ambiguity caused by
multi-parameter instances.

Dependent Types.

Dependently typed languages, e.g., Agda
(
Devriese and
Piessens 2011
)
and
Idris
(
Brady 2013
)
, include language features that are inspired by
type classes. Proving resolution coherence in a dependently
typed setting requires significant extension of our calculi, as dependent types
collapse the term and type levels into a single level and thus enable more powerful
type signatures for classes and instances.
Furthermore, our logical relation needs to be
extended to support dependent types
(
Bernardy
et al. 2012
)
as well.
Fortunately, the essence of our proof strategy still applies. That is, the
intermediate language incorporates separate binding structures for dictionaries,
and enforces the uniqueness of dictionaries. We thus believe a non-trivial
extension of our proof methodology can be used to prove coherence for type
class resolution in the setting of dependently typed languages.

Non-overlapping Instances.

Our work is built on top of the assumption that type class instances do not
overlap. This is enforced during the type checking of instance declarations, and
made explicit in the intermediate language. Whether a constraint is entailed
directly from an instance, through user provided constraints in a type
annotation, or through local evidence, is not actually relevant, as all evidence
ultimately has to originate from a non-overlapping instance declaration.

Therefore, our work can be extended to include features where the assumption
holds true.
This includes, among others, GADT’s
(
Peyton Jones et al. 2006
)
,
implication constraints
(
Bottu et al. 2017
)
, type constructors, higher
kinded types and constraint kinds
(
Orchard and
Schrijvers 2010
)
,
e.g.,
Bottu et al. 2017
informally discuss the coherence of implication
constraints based on the same assumption.
These features are all included in GHC.

Modules.

Modules, as supported by GHC, pose an interesting challenge, as they are known
to cause a form of
ambiguity.
4
4

4

http://blog.ezyang.com/2014/07/type-classes-confluence-coherence-global-uniqueness/

GHC does not statically check the uniqueness of instances across modules, thus
indirectly allowing users to write overlapping instances, as long as no
ambiguity arises during resolution.
Adapting our global uniqueness assumption to accommodate this additional freedom
remains an interesting challenge.

Laziness.

The operational semantics of the
{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{{D}}}}
and
{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{\lx@text@lbrace\lx@text@rbrace}}}
calculi in this work
are given through standard call-by-name semantics, in order to approximate
Haskell’s laziness. The system can easily be adapted to either call-by-value or
call-by-need, with little impact on the proofs.

It is important to note though, that while expressions are evaluated lazily, type
class resolution itself is eager, and constructs the full dictionaries at
compile time. This complicates supporting certain GHC features that rely on laziness, like
cyclic and infinite dictionaries. They could be supported
through loop detection and deferring the construction of
dictionaries to runtime, but these would nonetheless pose a significant challenge.

9.
Related Work

Type Classes.

Jones 1993
;
Jones 1994
formally proves coherence for the framework of qualified types,
which generalizes from type classes to arbitrary evidence-backed type
constraints. He focuses on nondeterminism in the typing derivation, and assumes
that resolution is coherent.

Morris 2014
presents an alternative, denotational
semantics for type classes (without superclasses) that avoids elaboration and
instead interprets qualified type schemes as the set of denotations of all its
monomorphic instantiations that satisfy the qualifiers. The nondeterminism of
resolution does not affect these semantics.

Kahl and
Scheffczyk 2001
present named type class instances that are not
used during resolution, but can be explicitly passed to functions. Nevertheless,
they violate the uniqueness of instances, and give rise to incoherence of the
form illustrated by our
discern
function in Section
2.3
.

Unlike most other languages with type classes (such as Haskell, Mercury or
PureScript) Coq
(
Sozeau and Oury 2008
)
does not enforce the non-overlapping instances
condition. Consequently, coherence does not hold for type class resolution in
Coq. The reason for this alternative design choice is twofold:

(a)

Since Coq’s type system is more complex than that found in regular
programming languages, it is not always possible to decide whether two
instances overlap
(
Lampropoulos and
Pierce 2018
, Chapter 2: Typeclasses)
.

(b)

Type class members in Coq are often proofs and, unlike for expressions,
users are often indifferent to coherence in the presence of proofs (even
though from a semantic point of view, Coq differentiates between them).
This concept is known as
“proof irrelevance”
(
Gilbert
et al. 2019
)
, that is, as long as at least one proof
exists, the concrete choice between these proofs is irrelevant.

Users can deal with this lack of coherence by either assigning priorities to
overlapping instances, or by manually curating the instance database and
locally removing specific instances.

Winant and
Devriese 2018
introduce explicit dictionary application to the Haskell
language, and prove coherence for this extended system.
Their proof is parametric in the constraint entailment judgment and thus assumes
that the constraint solver produces “canonical” evidence.
They proceed by introducing a disjointness condition to explicitly applied
dictionaries, in order to ensure that coherence is preserved by their extension.
Our paper proves their aforementioned assumption, by establishing coherence for
type class resolution.

Dreyer et al. 2007
blend ML modules with Haskell type
class resolution. Unlike Haskell, they feature multiple global (or outer)
scopes; instances within one such global scope must not overlap. Moreover,
global instances are shadowed by those given through type signatures. While
their language has been formalized, no formal proof of coherence is given.

Implicits.

Cochis
(
Schrijvers et al. 2019
)
is a calculus with highly expressive implicit resolution,
including local instances. It achieves coherence by imposing restrictions on
the implicit context and enforcing a deterministic resolution process. This allows
for a much simpler coherence proof.

OCaml’s modular implicits
(
White
et al. 2014
)
do not enforce
uniqueness of “instances” but dynamically ensure coherence by rejecting
programs where there are multiple possible resolution derivations. This
approach has not been formalized yet.

Other.

Reynolds
(
Reynolds 1991
)
introduced the notion of coherence in the
context of the Forsythe language’s intersection types; he proved coherence
directly in terms of the denotational semantics of the language.

In contrast,

Bi
et al. 2018
;
Bi
et al. 2019
consider a setting where subtyping for intersection types is
elaborated to coercions. Inspired by
Biernacki and
Polesiuk 2015
, they use an approach
based on contextual equivalence and logical relations, which has inspired us in turn.
However, they do not create an intermediate language to avoid the problem of a more
expressive target language. This leads to a notion of
contextual equivalence that straddles two languages and complicates their proofs.

10.
Conclusion

We have formally proven that type class resolution is coherent by means of
logical relations and an
intermediate language with explicit dictionaries.
In future work we would like to mechanize the proof and adapt it to extensions
such as quantified class constraints and GADT’s.

This work would not have been possible without the enlightening discussions with
Dominique Devriese and George Karachalias.
Furthermore, we would like to thank Alexander Vandenbroucke, Ruben Pieters and Steven Keuchel,
as well as the anonymous ICFP 2019 and Haskell Symposium 2018 reviewers,
for their constructive feedback.

Research (FWO) and the Hong Kong Research
Grant Council projects number 17210617 and 17258816.

}{}}}\frac{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma}}}}}\rightsquigarrow\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{\Gamma}}}}}}{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma}}},{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{a}}}}}\rightsquigarrow\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{\Gamma}}},{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{a}}}}}}\quad\textsc{right=\scriptsize{{\hypertarget{ottalt:rule:ott:Ctx-TVar}{{{Ctx-TVar}}}
}{}}}

In the translation mechanism, we have assumed namespace translation functions which take a

{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{{D}}}}
type, term or dictionary-variable name and return the same identifier
representing a
{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{\lx@text@lbrace\lx@text@rbrace}}}
type or term variable. There are four such functions, each with
a different namespace as domain:

Type variables:

It translates a type variable of the
{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{{D}}}}
language,

{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{a}}}
, to the
{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{\lx@text@lbrace\lx@text@rbrace}}}
type variable with the same name,
{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{a}}}
.

Term variables:

Similar to type variables, but for the term sort.

Dictionary variables:

It translates a dictionary variable,
{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\delta}}}
, to a
{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{\lx@text@lbrace\lx@text@rbrace}}}

term variable with the same name.

Dictionary labels:

It translates a dictionary method,
{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{m}}}
, to a record-field
label,
{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{m}}}
, with the same name.

This identifier translation is assumed in all judgments that involve elaboration, such as
the
{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{{D}}}}
term typing. When we regard identifiers, the font-color change
implies such a translation. However, this convention is not used in other language sorts
(types, non-variable terms, etc.). For example, two types with the same identifier but of
different color mean only two types, a
{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{{D}}}}
and a
{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{\lx@text@lbrace\lx@text@rbrace}}}
type, that are not related
to each other. Any specification of the relation between the two types is given by the
judgments they appear in.

Appendix G
Logical Relations

In the definitions for the logical relations below,
\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\gamma}}}}}=\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\gamma}}}^{\prime},{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\delta}}}\mapsto({\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{dv}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}},{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{dv}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}})}}
and
\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\phi}}}}}=\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\phi}}}^{\prime},{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{x}}}\mapsto({\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{e}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}},{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{e}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}})}}

are substitutions which map all dictionary variables
\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\delta}}}}}\in\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma}}}}}
and term
variables
\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{x}}}}}\in\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma}}}}}
onto two (possibly different) dictionary values and term
values respectively. Notation-wise, we adopted the convention that
{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\gamma}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}

maps the dictionary variable
{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\delta}}}
to the leftmost value
{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{dv}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}
and

{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\gamma}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}
substitutes
{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\delta}}}
for the rightmost value
{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{dv}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}
.
Similarly for
{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\phi}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}
and
{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\phi}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}
.

The third kind of substitution
\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{R}}}}}=\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{R}}}^{\prime},{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{a}}}\mapsto({\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\sigma}}},{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\mathit{r}}}})}}
maps all type variables

\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{a}}}}}\in\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma}}}}}
onto closed types
{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\sigma}}}
, while also storing a relation

{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\mathit{r}}}}
. This relation
{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\mathit{r}}}}
is an arbitrary member of the set of all
relations
\mathit{Rel}[\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\sigma}}}}}]
which offer the following property:

\mathit{Rel}[\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\sigma}}}}}]=\{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\mathit{r}}}}\in\mathcal{P}({\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{v}}}\times{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{v}}})\penalty\ |\penalty\ \forall({\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{v}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}},{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{v}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}})\in{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\mathit{r}}}}:\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\bullet}}\vdash_{tm}\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{v}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}}:\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\sigma}}}}}\wedge\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\bullet}}\vdash_{tm}\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{v}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}}:\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\sigma}}}}}\}

Appendix H
Strong Normalization Relations

As opposed to Section
G
, the relations and substitutions in the
strong normalization relations described below, are unary.
The substitutions
\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\gamma^{SN}}}}}}=\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\gamma^{SN}}}}^{\prime},{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\delta}}}\mapsto{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{d}}}}}
and

map all dictionary
variables

and term variables

onto
well-typed dictionaries
{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{d}}}
and expressions
\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{e}}}}}\in\mathcal{SN}\llbracket\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\sigma}}}}}\rrbracket^{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}}},\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}}}_{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{R^{SN}}}}}}}
. The final kind of substitution
\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{R^{SN}}}}}}=\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{R^{SN}}}}^{\prime},{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{a}}}\mapsto({\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\sigma}}},{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\mathit{r}}}})}}
maps all type variables
\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{a}}}}}\in\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma}}}}}
onto closed types
{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\sigma}}}
,
while also storing a relation
{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\mathit{r}}}}
.
This relation
{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\mathit{r}}}}
is an arbitrary member of the
set of all relations
\mathit{Rel}[\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\sigma}}}}}]
which offer the following property:

\mathit{Rel}[\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\sigma}}}}}]=\{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\mathit{r}}}}\in\mathcal{P}({\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{e}}})\penalty\ |\penalty\ \forall{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{e}}}\in{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\mathit{r}}}}:\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\bullet}}\vdash_{tm}\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{e}}}}}:\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\sigma}}}}}\}

We adopted the convention that
{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{R^{SN}}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}({\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{a}}})
maps the type variable

{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{a}}}
onto the closed type
{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\sigma}}}
and
{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{R^{SN}}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}({\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{a}}})
denotes the
contained set of expressions
{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\mathit{r}}}}
.

Proof.

This theorem is mutually proven with Theorems
6

and
7
. This mutual dependency is illustrated in
Figure
14
, where an arrow from A to B denotes A being
dependent on B. Note that at the dependency from
Theorem
7
to
1
, the size of

{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{P}}}
is strictly decreasing, whereas
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{P}}}
remains constant at every
other dependency. Consequently, the size of
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{P}}}
is strictly decreasing in
every possible cycle. The induction thus remains well-founded.

By applying Lemma
13
to the first
hypothesis, we get:

(1)

\vdash_{ctx}^{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{M}}}\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{P}}}}};\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma}}}}}\rightsquigarrow\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma}}}}}

We continue by induction on the lexicographic order of the tuple (size of the
expression, typing mode). Regarding typing mode, we define type checking to be
larger than type inference. In each mutual dependency, we know that the
tuple size decreases, meaning that the induction is well-founded.

\vdash_{ctx}^{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{M}}}\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\bullet}};\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma}}}}}\rightsquigarrow\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\bullet}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma}}}}}

then

.

Proof.

By induction on the lexicographic order of the tuple (size of

{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}
, the derivation height of type well-formedness and the constraint
well-formedness). In each mutual dependency, the size of the tuple is
decreasing, so we know that the induction is well-founded.

Theorem 6 (Typing Preservation - Constraints Proving).

If
\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{P}}}}};\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma}}}}}\vDash^{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{M}}}\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{Q}}}}}\rightsquigarrow\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{d}}}}}
,
and
\vdash_{ctx}^{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{M}}}\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{P}}}}};\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma}}}}}\rightsquigarrow\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma}}}}}
,
and
\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma}}}}}\vdash_{\mathit{Q}}^{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{M}}}\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{Q}}}}}\rightsquigarrow\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{Q}}}}}
,
then
\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma}}}}}\vdash_{d}\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{d}}}}}:\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{Q}}}}}
.

Proof.

By induction on the constraint resolution derivation tree.
This theorem is mutually proven with Theorems
1

and
7
(Figure
14
).
Note that at the dependency from
Theorem
7
to
1
, the size of

{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{P}}}
is strictly decreasing, whereas
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{P}}}
remains constant at every
other dependency. Consequently, the size of
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{P}}}
is strictly decreasing in
every possible cycle. The induction thus remains well-founded.

Theorem 7 (Typing Preservation - Environment Well-Formedness).

If
\vdash_{ctx}^{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{M}}}\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{P}}}}};\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{\Gamma}}}}}\rightsquigarrow\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma}}}}}
,
then
\vdash_{ctx}\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma}}}}}
.

Proof.

By induction on the well-formedness derivation.
This theorem is mutually proven with Theorems
1

and
6
(Figure
14
).
Note that at the dependency from
Theorem
7
to
1
, the size of

{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{P}}}
is strictly decreasing, whereas
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{P}}}
remains constant at every
other dependency. Consequently, the size of
{\color[rgb]{0,0.4297,0.7227}{{P}}}
is strictly decreasing in
every possible cycle. The induction thus remains well-founded.

Lemma 36 (Environment Well-Formedness Strengthening).

If
\vdash_{ctx}\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma}}}}}

then
\vdash_{ctx}\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\bullet}}
.

Proof.

By case analysis on the hypothesis,
the last rules used to construct it must be (possibly zero)
consecutive applications of
iCtx-MEnv
. Revert those rules, to obtain

\vdash_{ctx}\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\bullet}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma}}}}}
.
By further case analysis (with
iCtx-tyEnvTm
,
iCtx-tyEnvTy
and

iCtx-tyEnvD
), we get
\vdash_{ctx}\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\bullet}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\bullet}}
.
The goal follows by consecutively
re-applying rule
iCtx-MEnv
with the appropriate premises.

∎

Theorem 8 (Preservation).

If
\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma}}}}}\vdash_{tm}\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{e}}}}}:\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\sigma}}}}}
,
and
\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}}}\vdash\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{e}}}}}\longrightarrow\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{e}}}^{\prime}}}
,
then
\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma}}}}}\vdash_{tm}\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{e}}}^{\prime}}}:\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\sigma}}}}}
.

Proof.

By induction on the typing derivation.

iTm-true

{\frac{\vdash_{ctx}\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma}}}}}}{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma}}}}}\vdash_{tm}\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\mathit{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{True}}}}}:\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\mathit{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{Bool}}}}}}\quad\textsc{right=\scriptsize{{\hypertarget{ottalt:rule:ott:iTm-true}{{{iTm-true}}}
}{}}}}

\mathit{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{True}}}
is already a value, so impossible case.

iTm-false

{\frac{\vdash_{ctx}\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma}}}}}}{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma}}}}}\vdash_{tm}\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\mathit{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{False}}}}}:\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\mathit{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{Bool}}}}}}\quad\textsc{right=\scriptsize{{\hypertarget{ottalt:rule:ott:iTm-false}{{{iTm-false}}}
}{}}}}

\mathit{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{False}}}

K.4.
Strong Normalization

Theorem 10 (Strong Normalization).

If
\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\bullet}}\vdash_{tm}\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{e}}}}}:\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\sigma}}}}}

then all possible evaluation derivations for
{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{e}}}
terminate :

\exists{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{v}}}:\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}}}\vdash\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{e}}}}}\longrightarrow^{*}\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{v}}}}}
.

Proof.

By Theorem
11
and
12
, with
{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{R^{SN}}}}=\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\bullet}}
,
\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\phi^{SN}}}}}}=\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\bullet}}
,
\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\gamma^{SN}}}}}}=\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\bullet}}
, since
\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma}}}}}=\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\bullet}}
,
it follows that:

\exists{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{v}}}:\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}}}\vdash\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{e}}}}}\longrightarrow^{*}\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{v}}}}}

Furthermore, since evaluation in
{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{{D}}}}
is deterministic
(Lemma
41
), there is exactly 1
possible evaluation derivation. Consequently, all derivations terminate.

∎

\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{e}}}}}\in\mathcal{SN}\llbracket\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\sigma}}}}}\rrbracket^{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}}},\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}}}_{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{R^{SN}}}}}}}
,
then
\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\bullet}}\vdash_{tm}\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{e}}}}}:\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{R^{SN}}}}({\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\sigma}}})}}

Proof.

The goal is baked into the relation. It follows by simple induction on

{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\sigma}}}
.

Corollary 1 (Compositionality for Strong Normalization (Context Interpretation)).

Suppose
\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{R^{SN}}}}}}\in\mathcal{F^{SN}}\llbracket\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma}}}}}\rrbracket^{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}}},\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}}}
,
then
\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{e}}}}}\in\mathcal{SN}\llbracket\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\sigma}}}}}\rrbracket^{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}}},\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}}}_{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{R^{SN}}}}}}}

if and only if
\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{e}}}}}\in\mathcal{SN}\llbracket\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{R^{SN}}}}({\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\sigma}}})}}\rrbracket^{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}}},\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}}}_{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\bullet}}}
.

Proof.

The choices from
\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{R^{SN}}}}}}\in\mathcal{F^{SN}}\llbracket\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma}}}}}\rrbracket^{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}}},\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}}}
always satisfy the
precondition of Compositionality for Strong Normalization
(Lemma
49
). Therefore,
we can do
induction on
{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma}}}
and apply Compositionality for Strong Normalization
(Lemma
49
), in combination with the induction hypothesis,
to prove the goal.

If
\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma}}}}}\vdash_{tm}\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{e}}}}}:\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\sigma}}}}}

then

\frac{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma}}}}}\vdash\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}}:\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{e}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}}\simeq_{log}\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}}:\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{e}}}^{\prime}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}}:\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\sigma}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}\rightarrow{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\sigma}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}}\quad\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma}}}}}\vdash\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}}:\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{e}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}}\simeq_{log}\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}}:\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{e}}}^{\prime}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}}:\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\sigma}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}}}{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma}}}}}\vdash\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}}:\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{e}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}\,{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{e}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}}\simeq_{log}\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}}:\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{e}}}^{\prime}_{{\mathrm{1}}}\,{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{e}}}^{\prime}_{{\mathrm{2}}} Proof.

\displaystyle\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{R}}}}}\in\mathcal{F}\llbracket\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma}}}}}\rrbracket^{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}}}

\frac{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma}}},{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{a}}}}}\vdash\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}}:\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{e}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}}\simeq_{log}\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}}:\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{e}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}}:\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\sigma}}}}}}{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma}}}}}\vdash\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}}:\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Lambda{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{a}}}.{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{e}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}}\simeq_{log}\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}}:\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Lambda{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{a}}}.{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{e}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}}:\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\forall{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{a}}}.{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\sigma}}}}}}\quad\textsc{right=\scriptsize{}}

Proof.

Given
\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}}\vdash\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{e}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}}\longrightarrow\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{e}}}^{\prime}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}}

,

Theorem 22 (Expression Reflexivity).

If
\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma}}}}}\vdash_{tm}\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{e}}}}}:\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\sigma}}}}}

and
\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma}}}}}\vdash_{tm}\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{e}}}}}:\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\sigma}}}}}

and
\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}}\vdash\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}}\simeq_{log}\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}}
,
then
\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma}}}}}\vdash\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}}:\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{e}}}}}\simeq_{log}\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}}:\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{e}}}}}:\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\sigma}}}}}
.

and consequently, since

term typing
is syntax directed, on both typing derivations.

\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{e}}}}}=\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\mathit{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{True}}}}}
(
iTm-true
)

{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma}}}}}\vdash_{tm}\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\mathit{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{True}}}}}:\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\mathit{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{Bool}}}}}\wedge\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma}}}}}\vdash_{tm}\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\mathit{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{True}}}}}:\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\mathit{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{Bool}}}}}}

The goal to prove is the following:

\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma}}}}}\vdash\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}}:\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\mathit{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{True}}}}}\simeq_{log}\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}}:\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\mathit{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{True}}}}}:\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\mathit{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{Bool}}}}}

Proof.

The theorem is stated in a nested fashion, where all common hypotheses are introduced in the
outer statement. Each of the four inner statements extends the outer statement with two
context-typing hypotheses, and sets the conclusion of the theorem, which is identical for each of
the four cases.

Suppose expressions
\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{e}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}}
and
\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{e}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}}

Lemma 58 (Dictionary Elaboration Uniqueness).

If
\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma}}}}}\vdash_{\mathit{Q}}\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{Q}}}}}\,\rightsquigarrow\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{\sigma}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}}
and
\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma}}}}}\vdash_{\mathit{Q}}\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{Q}}}}}\,\rightsquigarrow\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{\sigma}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}}
,
then
\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{\sigma}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}}=\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{\sigma}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}}
.

Proof.

By straightforward induction on the well-formedness derivation.

N.3.
Determinism

Theorem 36 (Deterministic Dictionary Elaboration).

If
\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma}}}}}\vdash_{d}\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{d}}}}}:\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{Q}}}}}\,\rightsquigarrow\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{e}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}}

and
\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma}}}}}\vdash_{d}\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{d}}}}}:\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{Q}}}}}\,\rightsquigarrow\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{e}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}}
,
then
\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{e}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}}=\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{e}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}}
.

Proof.

This theorem is proved mutually with Theorem
37
. The proof follows
structural induction on both hypotheses.

If
\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma}}}}}\vdash_{tm}\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{e}}}}}:\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\sigma}}}}}\rightsquigarrow\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{e}}}_{{\mathrm{1}}}}}

\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma}}}}}\vdash_{tm}\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{e}}}}}:\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\sigma}}}}}\rightsquigarrow\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{e}}}_{{\mathrm{2}}}}}

Lemma 71 (
{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}\boldsymbol{F}_{\textbf{\lx@text@lbrace\lx@text@rbrace}}}
Preservation of Values).

If
\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\bullet}}\vdash_{tm}\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{v}}}}}:\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\sigma}}}}}\rightsquigarrow\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{e}}}}}

then
{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{e}}}
is a value.

Proof.

By straightforward case analysis on the typing derivation.

Theorem 40 (Value Semantic Preservation).

If
\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\bullet}}\vdash_{tm}\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{e}}}}}:\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\sigma}}}}}\rightsquigarrow\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{e}}}}}

and
\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}}}\vdash\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{e}}}}}\longrightarrow^{*}\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{v}}}}}

then
\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\bullet}}\vdash_{tm}\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{v}}}}}:\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\sigma}}}}}\rightsquigarrow\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{v}}}}}

and
\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{e}}}}}\simeq\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{v}}}}}
.

Proof.

From the Preservation Theorem
8
and Progress
Theorem
9
, in combination with the hypothesis,
we know that:

\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Sigma}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\Gamma_{C}}}}}};\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\bullet}}\vdash_{tm}\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{v}}}}}:\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{{\color[rgb]{0.2344,0.5,0.1914}{{\sigma}}}}}\rightsquigarrow\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{e}}}^{\prime}}}

Lemma
71
teaches us that
{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{e}}}^{\prime}

{\color[rgb]{0.7148,0.1953,0.1094}{{v}}}

The goal follows by repeatedly applying Theorem
